sections.html:
Montgomery, the state capital, is also the county seat. Population was 228,954 in 2020, a hair under the 229,363 recorded ten years earlier, and the 2025 estimate sits at 225,891. Of 105,293 housing units, 11.5% stood empty. Owners occupy 56.3% of homes that have residents, which leaves 43.7% as rentals. That renter share explains why inherited rentals and worn-out landlord houses turn up often in local resales.

Plenty of addresses fall outside any city. Pintlala, Snowdoun and Mount Meigs are unincorporated, while Hope Hull and Pike Road are towns. Two houses on similar-looking streets can carry different bills depending on the taxing area. Pin down yours before you discuss price with anyone.

One bill arrives each year, due October 1. Pay after December 31 and it counts as delinquent. A bill left alone moves through the schedule below.

MonthStage of an unpaid bill
October 1Bill comes due
January 1Bill is late
FebruaryHanded to probate court
MarchProbate court sits
AprilParcel advertised
MayProperty sold at tax sale

The lien date here is October 1 of the year before the tax year. So the fall bill describes who owned the property, and how it looked, twelve months earlier. An owner who is behind has until the spring advertisement to catch up before the sale process takes over. If you are unsure where your parcel stands, the county office can tell you in one phone call.

The county Board of Equalization decides assessment appeals. You have thirty days, counted from the date printed on the notice rather than the day it arrived, and filing is free.

  • Send your appeal to propertytaxappeals@mc-ala.org, or phone (334) 832-1327 for real property and (334) 832-1375 for personal property.
  • There is no required form, though the Board wants an original signature.
  • Attach evidence. Closing statements, appraisals, comparable sales and insurance values are the examples the county gives.
  • Ask for an informal review before the deadline. The county recommends it, and it can settle a simple error without a formal hearing.
  • An out-of-state agent can file for you, and you do not need a lawyer, provided the agent brings a signed authorization.

The sales used as comparisons come from a fixed period tied to your tax year, and your notice names the dates. The county's appraisal appeals FAQ walks through the same steps if you want them in writing. If you plan to sell soon and the value looks too high, file anyway, because a lower assessed value also trims the following bill.

To qualify for the state exemption, the home must be a single-family house that you own and occupy as your primary residence on the first day of the tax year, on no more than 160 acres. Apply at your county office.

  • Under 65 and not disabled: up to $4,000 of assessed value.
  • 65 or older: the state portion has no maximum.
  • Permanently and totally disabled: the state portion has no maximum.
  • Blind: the state portion has no maximum.

County exemptions run separately and come with income tests. A retiree should ask the county office which kind fits. The exemption follows the owner, so it ends when you sell and the buyer must file a fresh application. Expect the first bill after a sale to look higher for that reason.

sections.h2: What closing looks like at the courthouse
sections.html:
Filing the deed happens at the judge of probate's office. Alabama attaches a recordation tax, 50 cents for every $500 of value conveyed. If a mortgage already paid its own mortgage tax, that debt can be subtracted from the taxable amount. Recording staff want proof of the true price. Deliberately holding that proof back after being asked brings a penalty of $100 or 25% of the tax, whichever is higher.

Closing agents file the paperwork on your behalf, so you seldom visit the recording desk yourself. Expect to supply a government photo ID, the names exactly as they appear on the deed and the mailing address where tax notices should go after the sale. When the owner has died, the personal representative must be appointed before any deed can be signed. Appointment can run longer than the sale, which is a reason to begin it early.

A late bill will not stop you from selling. It only affects who gets paid first at the table. A workable order:

  1. Phone the county and get the amount owed on the parcel, counting anything already delinquent.
  2. Collect the deed, your most recent tax bill, a payoff letter from the mortgage lender and a plain list of repairs you already know the house needs.
  3. Instruct the title company to pay the tax balance from your proceeds, and ask for a line showing it on the settlement statement.
  4. Work out who signs: every owner named on the deed, plus a personal representative where an owner has died.
  5. After liens are cleared, the closing agent files the deed with the probate judge.

A bill that has reached probate court costs more than the original tax, so request a fresh payoff figure before you say yes to any offer. Because the property is exposed once the May sale arrives, owners with a late bill tend to act fast.

Common situations here include an inherited house, a rental with a tenant inside, repairs that were put off for years and a tax bill that slipped. A cash purchase that closes as-is can work for these because there are no repair bids, no open houses and no wait on a buyer's loan.

  • Inherited homes: heirs who live elsewhere may not want a drawn-out probate listing.
  • Rentals: you can sell without emptying the unit first.
  • Back taxes: the balance can come out of the sale proceeds.
  • Older houses: nobody asks for a repair list before an as-is closing.

Cash Home Buyers looks at Montgomery County houses exactly as they stand and replies with a written offer. You make the call, and saying no costs nothing. When you request the offer, have the tax bill and deed on hand so the number accounts for what is owed.

Before you decide, set the offer beside two other numbers. One is what a listing might bring after repairs, agent fees and months of showings. The other is what you still owe on the mortgage and taxes. If a probate or tax deadline is close, the calendar can matter more than a few thousand dollars of price. Ask the buyer when closing could happen and who pays for the title work, then get both answers in writing before you sign.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to appeal an assessment in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: Nothing. The Board of Equalization charges no filing fee, but the appeal has to arrive within thirty days of the date on your notice.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Montgomery County, Alabama?
faqs.a: October 1. They go delinquent after December 31, and unpaid accounts head toward probate court and a tax sale in May.

faqs.q: Who handles assessment appeals in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: The Board of Equalization, working with the county Appraisal Department. For real property, write to propertytaxappeals@mc-ala.org or call (334) 832-1327.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Montgomery County house with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes. Get the payoff amount from the county and ask the title company to pay it from your proceeds. A cash buyer can often build that payoff into the deal.

faqs.q: Do I need an attorney to file an appeal?
faqs.a: No. An attorney is optional, and an out-of-state agent can file as well if the agent supplies a signed authorization.
